question: According to the manual, sleeping 6 hours or less before driving does what to your crash risk?
choice_b: Doubles your risk
choice_d: Cuts your risk in half
explanation: The manual lists being sleep-deprived or fatigued (6 hours of sleep or less) as a risk factor that triples your risk of a fall-asleep crash.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-24

question: If you notice signs of fatigue while driving, the manual recommends you:
choice_a: Turn up the radio and keep driving
choice_b: Open a window and drink caffeine to push through
choice_c: Stop driving and sleep for the night, or take a 15-20 minute nap
choice_d: Increase your speed to reach your destination sooner
explanation: If you notice any signs of fatigue, you should stop driving and go to sleep for the night or take a 15-20 minute nap.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-24

question: At night, approximately how far ahead can you see with low beam headlights compared to high beams?
choice_a: About 100 feet with low beams, 150 feet with high beams
choice_b: About 250 feet with low beams, 350-500 feet with high beams
choice_c: About 500 feet with low beams, 1,000 feet with high beams
choice_d: There is no difference between low and high beam range
explanation: With low beams you can see ahead about 250 feet, and with high beams about 350-500 feet; you must adjust speed so you can stop within your sight distance.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-25

question: You should dim your headlights when you are within how many feet of an oncoming vehicle or a vehicle you are following?
choice_b: 200 feet
choice_d: 1,000 feet
explanation: Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet, to avoid blinding other drivers.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-26

question: According to the manual, what is the best advice for driving in fog?
choice_a: Use your high beams for maximum visibility
choice_b: Don't drive; pull off the road until visibility improves
choice_c: Speed up to get through the fog bank quickly
choice_d: Follow closely behind another vehicle's taillights
explanation: The best advice for driving in fog is don't; it is preferable to pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility is better. If you must drive, use low-beam headlights and fog lights, not high beams.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-26

question: If you must drive in fog, the manual advises you to turn on your 4-way emergency flashers primarily to:
choice_a: Comply with a universal legal requirement in all states
choice_b: Give vehicles approaching from behind a quicker chance to notice your vehicle
choice_c: Warn oncoming traffic to move over
choice_d: Save battery power compared to headlights
explanation: Turning on your 4-way flashers in fog gives vehicles approaching you from behind a quicker opportunity to notice your vehicle.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-26

question: While driving in winter conditions, a lack of spray or splash from vehicles ahead of you on a wet-looking road is a sign that:
choice_a: The road has just been salted
choice_b: Ice has likely formed on the road
choice_d: Your tires need more air pressure
explanation: A lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed on the road; you should also check your mirrors and wiper blades for ice.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-27

question: On slippery winter roads, why should you avoid using the engine brake or speed retarder?
choice_b: It can cause the driving wheels to skid on the slippery surface
choice_c: It is illegal in all states during winter
choice_d: It damages the transmission permanently
explanation: On slippery surfaces, don't use the engine brake or speed retarder because they can cause the driving wheels to skid.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-27

question: In very hot weather, how often should you inspect your tires?
choice_a: Once at the start of the trip only
choice_b: Every two hours or every 100 miles
choice_d: Only when a tire looks visibly low
explanation: You should inspect the tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather, since air pressure and heat build up.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-28

question: Why should you never remove a radiator cap on a pressurized cooling system until the engine has cooled?
choice_b: Steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns
choice_c: It will trigger the check-engine light
choice_d: It has no real danger, it's just a precaution
explanation: Never remove the radiator cap or any part of the pressurized system until it has cooled; steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-28

question: At a passive railroad-highway crossing (one with no traffic control device), who decides whether it is safe to stop or proceed?
choice_b: The decision rests entirely with the driver
choice_d: A crossing guard is always present
explanation: At a passive crossing, there is no traffic control device, so the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely in the driver's hands, requiring the driver to search for trains and judge if it is safe to cross.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-29

question: If there is no white stop line at a cross-buck sign, vehicles that are required to stop must stop no closer than 15 feet, and no farther than how many feet, from the nearest rail?
choice_b: 50 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: Vehicles required to stop at a cross-buck sign with no painted stop line must stop no closer than 15 feet or more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the nearest track.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-29

question: According to the manual, a typical tractor-trailer unit needs at least how many seconds to clear a single railroad track?
choice_b: 9 seconds
choice_d: 20 seconds
explanation: It takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track, and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-30

question: What should you never do while crossing railroad tracks?
choice_b: Shift gears
choice_d: Keep both hands on the wheel
explanation: Do not shift gears while crossing railroad tracks, as this could cause the vehicle to stall or hang up on the tracks.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-30

question: What happens to a vehicle's brakes if they are used too much on a long downgrade and become too hot?
choice_b: They can 'fade,' requiring harder application until you may not be able to slow or stop
choice_c: They automatically engage the parking brake
choice_d: Nothing, modern brakes cannot overheat
explanation: If brakes become too hot, they may start to 'fade,' meaning you have to apply them harder and harder to get the same stopping power, and can continue fading until you cannot slow down or stop at all.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-31

question: What is the purpose of an escape ramp on a steep mountain downgrade?
choice_a: To provide a shortcut to the bottom of the grade
choice_b: To safely stop runaway vehicles without injuring drivers and passengers
choice_c: To allow trucks to bypass weigh stations
choice_d: To provide a rest area for drivers
explanation: Escape ramps are built on many steep mountain downgrades to stop runaway vehicles safely, often using a long bed of loose, soft material, sometimes combined with an upgrade.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-32

question: Why should you avoid applying the brake while making a quick emergency turn?
choice_b: It's easy to lock your wheels while turning, which can cause you to skid out of control
choice_d: It has no real effect either way
explanation: Do not apply the brake while you are turning. It's very easy to lock your wheels while turning, and if that happens, you may skid out of control.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-32

question: Which emergency stopping method involves applying the brakes all the way and releasing them when the wheels lock up, then reapplying as soon as they start rolling again?
choice_b: Stab braking
choice_d: Engine braking
explanation: Stab braking involves applying your brakes all the way and releasing them when the wheels lock up; as soon as the wheels start rolling, you apply the brakes fully again.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-33

question: If your brakes fail while descending a long downgrade, what is your best hope for stopping the vehicle safely?
choice_b: Using an escape ramp, if one is available
choice_d: Steering into oncoming traffic to slow down
explanation: Any driver who loses brakes going downhill should use an escape ramp if it's available; ramps are usually located a few miles from the top of the downgrade.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-34

question: When a tire fails while driving, what should you do immediately?
choice_a: Brake hard to stop as quickly as possible
choice_b: Hold the steering wheel firmly and stay off the brake until the vehicle has slowed
choice_d: Swerve sharply to the shoulder
explanation: When a tire fails, hold the steering wheel firmly with both hands and stay off the brake, since braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control. Brake gently only after the vehicle has slowed.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-34

question: Which vehicles are required by the Department of Transportation to have ABS if built on or after March 1, 1997?
choice_b: Truck tractors with air brakes
choice_d: School buses only
explanation: The Department of Transportation requires ABS on truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-34

question: Which statement about ABS is accurate?
choice_a: ABS always shortens your stopping distance
choice_b: ABS lets you drive faster and follow more closely
choice_c: ABS helps you maintain steering control but does not necessarily shorten stopping distance
choice_d: ABS replaces the need for normal brakes
explanation: You may or may not be able to stop faster with ABS, but you should be able to steer around an obstacle while braking; ABS is an addition to, not a replacement for, your normal brakes.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-35

question: Which of the following is NOT listed as one of the four ways a skid is typically caused?
choice_b: Over-steering
choice_d: Under-inflated spare tire
explanation: Skids are caused by over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, or driving too fast for conditions; an under-inflated spare tire is not one of the listed causes.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-35

question: To correct a drive-wheel braking skid, you should:
choice_a: Apply the brakes harder to regain traction
choice_b: Stop braking to let the rear wheels roll again, and counter-steer
choice_c: Accelerate hard to pull out of the skid
choice_d: Turn the steering wheel in the direction the rear of the vehicle is sliding and hold it there
explanation: To correct a drive-wheel braking skid, stop braking to let the rear wheels roll again and keep them from sliding, then counter-steer as the vehicle turns back on course.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-36

question: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident scene, according to the manual?
choice_a: Call your dispatcher, take photos, exchange insurance information
choice_b: Protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured
choice_c: Move all vehicles immediately, direct traffic, call a tow truck
choice_d: Assess fault, file a report, contact your employer
explanation: The basic steps to be taken at any accident are to protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-37

question: If a cargo fire occurs in a van or box trailer carrying hazardous materials, why should you keep the doors shut?
choice_a: Opening the doors will supply the fire with oxygen and can cause it to burn very fast
choice_b: It is required to preserve evidence for the insurance claim
choice_c: Opening the doors voids the cargo insurance
choice_d: It keeps the smoke from setting off the smoke detector
explanation: For a cargo fire in a van or box trailer, keep the doors shut, especially if the cargo contains hazardous materials, because opening the doors supplies oxygen and can cause the fire to burn very fast.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-38

question: What is the key difference between a B:C fire extinguisher and an A:B:C fire extinguisher?
choice_b: A:B:C is designed to work on burning wood, paper, and cloth in addition to electrical fires and burning liquids
choice_d: B:C extinguishers are only for use on tires
explanation: The B:C type extinguisher is designed for electrical fires and burning liquids, while the A:B:C type is designed to also work on burning wood, paper, and cloth.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-38

question: According to the manual, roughly how much alcohol can the liver process per hour?
choice_b: About one-third of an ounce
choice_d: There is no limit; it depends only on body weight
explanation: The liver can only process about one-third an ounce of alcohol per hour, which is considerably less than the alcohol in a standard drink; only time, not coffee or a cold shower, will sober you up.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-39

question: According to the manual, drinking alcohol and driving contributes to over how many traffic deaths every year?
explanation: People who drink alcohol are involved in traffic accidents resulting in over 20,000 deaths every year, according to the manual.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-39

question: If you become too ill to safely operate a commercial motor vehicle, what does the manual say you should do?
choice_a: Drive slower than usual until you feel better
choice_b: You must not drive, except in an emergency, to the nearest place you can safely stop
choice_c: Ask a passenger without a CDL to take over driving
choice_d: Continue driving if the trip is nearly finished
explanation: If you become too ill to operate a motor vehicle safely, you must not drive; however, in case of an emergency, you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-40

question: A vehicle placarded for hazardous materials must have at least how many identical placards, placed on the front, rear, and both sides?
choice_b: Three
choice_d: Six
explanation: A placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, put on the front, rear, and both sides, each at least 10 3/4 inches square and readable from all four directions.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-41

question: Where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers while driving?
choice_b: In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach
choice_c: Anywhere in the cab, as long as they are somewhere in the vehicle
choice_d: Locked in the trailer with the cargo
explanation: Shipping papers must be kept in a pouch on the driver's door, in clear view within reach while driving, or on the driver's seat when the driver is out of the vehicle.
source_note: Arizona Commercial Driver License Manual (AAMVA 2005/2022 CDL Testing System, ADOT MVD, Revised 01/2026), Section 2 - Driving Safely, p. 2-41
